assessment_summary: I attempted to prove the statement, but the claim itself is fundamentally false. Any proof attempt would fail when asserting that the conditions of being Eulerian (connected, all even degrees) and 2-connected (no single cut vertex) are sufficient to guarantee a Hamiltonian cycle. A counterexample is the complete bipartite graph K_{2,3} with an additional edge between the two vertices in the part of size 2. This graph meets all conditions but fails the necessary condition for Hamiltonicity.
counterexample:
Let G be a graph with vertices V = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and edges E = {{1,4}, {1,5}, {2,4}, {2,5}, {3,4}, {3,5}, {4,5}}. 

- Eulerian: The degrees are deg(1)=deg(2)=deg(3)=2 and deg(4)=deg(5)=4. All degrees are even, and the graph is connected, so it is Eulerian.
- 2-connected: The graph has 5 vertices. Deleting any single vertex leaves a connected graph (e.g., deleting vertex 4 leaves 1, 2, 3 all connected to 5). Thus, it is 2-connected.
- Not Hamiltonian: A Hamiltonian cycle must visit all vertices. If we remove the set of vertices S = {4, 5} (which has size 2), the remaining graph consists of vertices {1, 2, 3} with no edges, which is 3 connected components. A well-known necessary condition for Hamiltonicity is that deleting any set S of vertices can leave at most |S| connected components. Since 3 > 2, the graph is not Hamiltonian. (Alternatively, vertices 1, 2, 3 all have degree 2, so a Hamiltonian cycle would have to use all 6 of their incident edges, which would require the cycle to have degree 3 at vertices 4 and 5, impossible for a cycle).
